Robust fluctuating intertwined charge stripes in the Emery model

Rong Zhang Email: rozhang@stanford.edu Affiliation: Department of Applied Physics, Stanford University, Stanford, CA 94305, USA Affiliation: Stanford Institute for Materials and Energy Sciences, SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory, 2575 Sand Hill Road, Menlo Park, CA 94025, USA    Sijia Zhao Affiliation: Department of Applied Physics, Stanford University, Stanford, CA 94305, USA Affiliation: Stanford Institute for Materials and Energy Sciences, SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory, 2575 Sand Hill Road, Menlo Park, CA 94025, USA    Hong-Chen Jiang Affiliation: Stanford Institute for Materials and Energy Sciences, SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory, 2575 Sand Hill Road, Menlo Park, CA 94025, USA    Brian Moritz Affiliation: Stanford Institute for Materials and Energy Sciences, SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory, 2575 Sand Hill Road, Menlo Park, CA 94025, USA    Edwin W. August 24, 2026
Abstract

The single-band Hubbard model is one of the most extensively studied models in condensed matter physics, giving rise to intertwined spin and charge stripes that coexist with, or lie in the vicinity of, superconductivity in the phase diagram. However, whether the low energy physics of the single-band Hubbard model is fully equivalent to the multi-band (multi-orbital) Emery model remains an unsettled question. While the intertwined stripes and nematicity have been studied in the single-band Hubbard model, a comprehensive picture in the Emery model is lacking. In this paper, we focus on the less investigated intertwined charge stripes using complementary density matrix renormalization group (DMRG) and determinant quantum Monte Carlo (DQMC) techniques. Our ground state DMRG confirms the presence of the oxygen-centered charge stripes at a reduced amplitude in the Emery model parameter regime widely used in the study of intertwined stripes. Close analysis of the oxygen orbital structure of the static charge correlation function from DQMC reveals the charge stripe pattern in real-space, showcasing stronger charge density modulation on pp-orbitals pointing along “the rivers of charge”, consistent with DMRG. For the parameter set with the largest fermion signs, we managed to reach a temperature where the system first demonstrated tendencies to form purely unidirectional spin and charge stripes, and the B1​gB_{1g} component becomes dominant in the bond-charge nematic susceptibility. This observation correlates with the doping dependence of the kinetic energy anisotropy, suggesting a close relation between the nematicity and charge stripes in the Emery model.

I Introduction

A long-standing problem in condensed matter physics is an understanding of intertwined orders and the way in which many candidate ground states emerge from simple models containing electron correlations. None has been more studied than the single band Hubbard model - simply containing electron kinetic energy of bandwidth W=8​tW=8t, with tt the nearest neighbor hopping, and an on-site-only Coulomb interaction parametrized by the Hubbard UU. While perturbative regions (both U/W<<1U/W<<1 for any doping, and W/U<<1W/U<<1 near half-filling) have enabled well-controlled studies via renormalization group and projected Hilbert space methods, respectively, intermediate values of U/WU/W have been the realm of numerical studies using many methods [1]. Density-matrix renormalization group (DMRG) methods likely have provided the most detailed window into the important ground-state ordering tendencies at short to intermediate length scales. In this region many candidate ground states have emerged - such as spin density waves, charge density waves, dx2−y2d_{x^{2}-y^{2}} superconductivity, as well as intertwined variants with a superposition of these orders - all appear to have ground state energies that can be separated by one part in a thousand of the hopping tt. If we make a rough estimate with photoemission on the cuprate materials - as a candidate system thought to be related to the Hubbard model - t∼250t\sim 250 meV and the ground states are separated by only a few degrees Kelvin. This has provided a challenge to the field, where numerical methods have predicted that either intertwined stripes or superconductivity may prevail at the lowest temperatures [3].

Yet, the single-band Hubbard model is only a rough proxy for the cuprates. Viewed as charge-transfer insulators at half-filling from numerous experimental characterizations, early theoretical attempts to mimic the cuprates stemmed from multi-band Hubbard models involving copper and oxygen degrees of freedom. [5] Foundational studies focused on whether a salient “bare minimum model” could be established, and whether this model contained separate oxygen and copper degrees of freedom. A key finding of the time, albeit still controversial today, is that a so-called Zhang-Rice singlet (ZRS) [33] - a combination of a hole on oxygen orbiting a hole on copper with a definite phase convention - would be sufficient enough to form a building block for broader models where the singlet could be treated as a single “doped hole” away from half-filling. Despite being well-known that the ZRS cannot be defined as a bound object over the entire Brillouin zone, it was reasonable to conclude that as far as the low-energy degrees of freedom are concerned, as long as a Fermi surface lay close to the anti-ferromagnetic zone boundary where the ZRS is well defined, a single-band Hubbard model may be sufficient.

In the years that followed, this issue has never been “settled”. Indeed, given the strong sensitivity of numerical studies to intertwined ground states, a fundamental question has lingered as to whether more realistic models for the cuprates - including oxygen degrees of freedom that are captured over the entire Brillouin zone - might show more definitive stability towards one of the numerous phases observed in single-band Hubbard model simulations at intermediate values of U/WU/W.

Despite the larger Hilbert space dimensions, DMRG studies have already weighed in on this issue on snorter ladders. It was found on 2-leg [27, 10, 31] and 4-leg ladders [29, 8, 25, 11] that bond-centered charge stripes are largely dominant across different hole dopings, resembling stripes in the single-band Hubbard model. These stripes have charge periods following that of half-filled stripes λ∼1/(2​p)\lambda\sim 1/(2p), with pp the doped hole concentration, and antiferromagnetic regions of Cu hole spins separated by domain walls, whereby the pp doped holes are strongly concentrated on oxygen orbitals. The ground state of the 2-leg ladders or cylinders is sensitive to boundary conditions and oxygen configurations [24], which affect the pairing between doped carriers. When dd-wave superconducting order is not the ground state, the introduction of longer-ranged hoppings or attractive next-nearest neighbor interactions lead to a uniform dd-wave superconductor [31] or pair-density wave [10], respectively. The 2-leg ladders were also shown to have [20, 21, 22] a loop current phase but outside of the realistic cuprate parameter range.

Issue with the fermion sign have not precluded studies using numerically exact quantum Monte Carlo methods [4, 12, 23]. Studies on the tendencies to dd-wave superconductivity indicate that the Emery model is promising [13, 16, 34], but are often inconclusive due to problematic fermion signs limiting consideration to high temperatures or weaker interactions than the physically relevant ones. Nevertheless, spin stripes on the copper dd-orbitals have been found for temperatures onsetting around T∼JT\sim J, the antiferromagnetic exchange, and persist over a wide doping range[8]. Further, tendencies to form charge stripes have been observed, possibly commensurate with the spin stripe on the oxygen orbitals[17]. However, the signal was found to be weaker compared to the charge correlation functions between the copper dd-orbitals. So far, an understanding of intertwined stripes in the Emery model is still at an early stage compared to that of the single-band Hubbard model, where DQMC simulations have captured fluctuating intertwined spin and charge stripes [6, 7] and strong nematic fluctuations [15], likely related to the charge stripes [19].

Given the greater degree of tunability present in the Emery model, where Coulomb interactions on both Cu and O can be varied and the degree of hybridization can be modified via the charge transfer energy, it is the goal of the present study to understand how spin and charge stripes - the predominant ordering tendencies in the single band Hubbard model - may be altered by parameter choices. Due again to the fermion sign, we limit focus to the accessible spin and charge density correlations, and examine in greater detail how oxygen charge order is manifest in different parameter regimes. Although the model is closer to the cuprates, and it is tempting to draw analogies to the behavior of clustered oxygen modulations seen in STM measurements at low temperatures [32], our study is more motivated from the numerical point of view for the temperatures that we can access.

In this work, we comprehensively study the fluctuating intertwined charge stripe tendency on the oxygen orbitals using numerically exact unbiased DQMC simulations and ground state DMRG simulations. By comparison with the single-band Hubbard model, our results show a richer structure of charge and spin stripes in the Emery model, with noticeable modifications by changing the Coulomb interactions. We found that ground state spin and charge stripes are qualitatively similar across the different parameters, but the standard Emery model parameter has a stronger charge modulation amplitude and displays a clearer charge stripe commensurate with the spin stripe in static correlation functions in DQMC simulations. The densities on the pp-orbitals oriented along the antiferromagnetic domain wall have the strongest modulation amplitude in DMRG, which corroborates our DQMC observation where linear response theory suggests that an impurity on pp-orbitals in one direction could induce a charge modulation in the other direction. For parameters with the best fermion sign, we observed a temperature at which the B1​gB_{1g} nematic susceptibility begins to dominate as the B2​gB_{2g} susceptibility dies off, and the static correlation functions on a square lattice start to show the superposition of unidirectional stripes. Along with the doping dependence of the kinetic energy anisotropy on rectangular lattices, our results suggest a close relationship between charge stripes and nematicity.

The outline of the paper is as follows. Sec. II specifies the Emery model and three different parameter sets we choose to simulate, relevant to cuprates and used previously in the literature. Sec. III defines correlation functions and susceptibilities. Sec. IV.1 presents the DMRG benchmark for the parameter set with smaller Ud​dU_{dd} and large JJ. Sec. IV.2 interprets the three different components of the oxygen charge correlation functions and the doping dependence of the modulation wavevector. Sec. IV.3 discusses the temperature evolution of the spin and charge stripe patterns, and the bond-charge nematicity, which indicates the tendency for kinetic energy anisotropy.

II Model

The three-band Hubbard model describes the CuO2 plane in hole language. It consists of copper-centered dx2−y2d_{x^{2}-y^{2}} orbitals arranged on a square lattice, and oxygen-centered pxp_{x} or pyp_{y} orbitals between every pair of nearest-neighbor copper sites, forming σ\sigma-bonds with the dx2−y2d_{x^{2}-y^{2}} orbital. The Emery model captures the nearest-neighbor hopping tp​dt_{pd} between pp and dd orbitals, and the hopping tp​pt_{pp} between pxp_{x} and pyp_{y} orbitals. UiU_{i} is the onsite Hubbard repulsion. Specifically, Ui=Ud​dU_{i}=U_{dd} for copper sites and Up​pU_{pp} for oxygen sites, and Δp​d\Delta_{pd} represents the charge transfer energy between the copper and oxygen orbitals. The chemical potential μ\mu is tuned to give various doping levels. The Hamiltonian consists of kinetic energy KK, charge transfer energy, and the Hubbard interaction energy. In the grand canonical ensemble, the Hamiltonian is given by

H=K+Δp​d​∑i,σni,σ+∑iUi​ni,↑​ni,↓−μ​∑i,σni,σ,K=−∑itp​d(ξai+ξbi+ξci+ξdi)−∑itp​p​(ξie+ξif+ξig+ξih),\displaystyle\begin{split}H&=K+\Delta_{pd}\sum_{i,\sigma}n_{i,\sigma}+\sum_{i}U_{i}n_{i,\uparrow}n_{i,\downarrow}-\mu\sum_{i,\sigma}n_{i,\sigma},\\ K&=-\sum_{i}t_{pd}(\xi^{a}_{i}+\xi^{b}_{i}+\xi^{c}_{i}+\xi^{d}_{i})\\ -&\sum_{i}t_{pp}(\xi^{e}_{i}+\xi^{f}_{i}+\xi^{g}_{i}+\xi^{h}_{i}),\end{split}

where the orbital sign convention is given by the following, as in [12]

ξia\displaystyle\xi^{a}_{i} =∑σ(pi,σx†di,σ+h.c.),\displaystyle=\sum_{\sigma}(p^{x\dagger}_{i,\sigma}d_{i,\sigma}+h.c.),
ξib\displaystyle\xi^{b}_{i} =−∑σ(pi,σy†di,σ+h.c.),\displaystyle=-\sum_{\sigma}(p^{y\dagger}_{i,\sigma}d_{i,\sigma}+h.c.),
ξic\displaystyle\xi^{c}_{i} =−∑σ(pi−𝐱^,σx†di,σ+h.c.),\displaystyle=-\sum_{\sigma}(p^{x\dagger}_{i-\hat{\mathbf{x}},\sigma}d_{i,\sigma}+h.c.),
ξid\displaystyle\xi^{d}_{i} =∑σ(pi−𝐲^,σy†di,σ+h.c.),\displaystyle=\sum_{\sigma}(p^{y\dagger}_{i-\hat{\mathbf{y}},\sigma}d_{i,\sigma}+h.c.),
ξie\displaystyle\xi^{e}_{i} =−∑σ(pi,σx†pi+x^−y^,σy+h.c.),\displaystyle=-\sum_{\sigma}(p^{x\dagger}_{i,\sigma}p_{i+\hat{x}-\hat{y},\sigma}^{y}+h.c.),
ξif\displaystyle\xi^{f}_{i} =∑σ(pi,σx†pi−y^,σy+h.c.),\displaystyle=\sum_{\sigma}(p^{x\dagger}_{i,\sigma}p_{i-\hat{y},\sigma}^{y}+h.c.),
ξig\displaystyle\xi^{g}_{i} =−∑σ(pi,σx†pi,σy+h.c.),\displaystyle=-\sum_{\sigma}(p^{x\dagger}_{i,\sigma}p_{i,\sigma}^{y}+h.c.),
ξih\displaystyle\xi^{h}_{i} =∑σ(pi,σx†pi+𝐱^,σy+h.c.).\displaystyle=\sum_{\sigma}(p^{x\dagger}_{i,\sigma}p_{i+\hat{\mathbf{x}},\sigma}^{y}+h.c.).

The summation index ii in the kinetic energy KK runs through all unit cells; in the charge transfer and chemical potential terms, it runs through all sites on the Lieb lattice where ni,σn_{i,\sigma} is the local density operator for spin σ\sigma at each site. A standard parameter set for the Emery model, nominally describing cuprates, is tp​d=1.13,tp​p=0.49,Δp​d=3.24,Ud​d=8.5t_{pd}=1.13,t_{pp}=0.49,\Delta_{pd}=3.24,U_{dd}=8.5, and Up​p=4.1U_{pp}=4.1 or 0.00.0, each in units of eV [12]. An alternative set of parameters used in DQMC studies of spin stripes [8, 17] has Ud​d=6​eU_{dd}=6~eV, Up​p=0U_{pp}=0, Δp​d=3​e\Delta_{pd}=3~eV, and is otherwise the same as the standard parameters. Here, Up​p=4.1U_{pp}=4.1 eV, Up​p=0U_{pp}=0, and Ud​d=6U_{dd}=6 eV distinguish the three parameter sets we study in this work.

Presumably, the effective antiferromagnetic coupling JJ is an important energy scale for stripe physics and Ud​d=6U_{dd}=6 eV has been used in studies of spin stripes due to the larger JJ. If we take the peak position of the spin dynamical structure factor S⁡(𝐪=(0,π),ω)S(\mathbf{q}=(0,\pi),\omega) from DQMC simulations at the lowest accessible temperature as an estimate for 2​J2J for each parameter set, the standard parameter set would have 2​JUp​p=4.1∼0.279​e2J_{U_{pp}=4.1}\sim 0.279~eV [34] at a lowest accessible temperature β=6.5​e\beta=6.5~eV-1, T/JUp​p=4.1∼1.1T/J_{U_{pp}=4.1}\sim 1.1, the same order of magnitude as the antiferromagnetic exchange, The other set has a much larger exchange coupling 2​JUd​d=6∼0.576​e2J_{U_{dd}=6}\sim 0.576~eV [8], and the fermion sign is also better, allowing for simulations to significantly lower temperatures, β=12​e\beta=12~eV-1 T/JUd​d=6∼0.29T/J_{U_{dd}=6}\sim 0.29, well below the exchange interaction scale.

III Method

III.1 Charge and spin correlation and susceptibilities

At finite temperatures, in linear response theory, the charge modulation induced by a perturbation on the local chemical potential is given by the connected static charge correlation function, and the spin modulation induced by a local magnetic field is given by the static spin correlation functions, which are defined as

χc,i​j​(ω=0)\displaystyle\chi_{c,ij}(\omega=0) =∫0β(⟨ni​(τ)​nj​(0)⟩−⟨ni​(τ)⟩​⟨nj​(0)⟩)​𝑑τ,\displaystyle=\int_{0}^{\beta}\left(\braket{n_{i}(\tau)n_{j}(0)}-\braket{n_{i}(\tau)}\braket{n_{j}(0)}\right)d\tau,
χs,i​j​(ω=0)\displaystyle\chi_{s,ij}(\omega=0) =∫0β⟨Siz​(τ)​Sjz​(0)⟩​𝑑τ,\displaystyle=\int_{0}^{\beta}\braket{S^{z}_{i}(\tau)S^{z}_{j}(0)}d\tau,

where β\beta is the inverse temperature, i,ji,j are different sites in real space, which could belong to different orbitals. We denote the real space correlation functions between two orbitals μ,ν\mu,\nu by χc,i​jμ​ν​(ω=0)\chi_{c,ij}^{\mu\nu}(\omega=0).

Well studied in previous work [8, 17], the spin correlation is most significant on copper dd-orbitals. For identifying the period of the spin stripes from real space, we focus on the staggered spin correlation on copper dd-orbitals, which is defined as

χs,i​j∗​(ω=0)\displaystyle\chi_{s,ij}^{*}(\omega=0) =(−1)(𝐫𝐢−𝐫j)⋅(x^+y^)​χs,i​j​(ω=0),\displaystyle=(-1)^{(\mathbf{r_{i}}-\mathbf{r}_{j})\cdot(\hat{x}+\hat{y})}\chi_{s,ij}(\omega=0),

where the i,ji,j are dd orbital indices.

Real space correlation functions that possess C4C_{4} symmetry, such as the spin correlations on dd orbital, or pxp_{x}-pyp_{y} charge correlation functions, should show patterns corresponding to the momentum space superposition of the modulation wavevectors of stripes related by symmetry, as discussed in the Supplementary information of Ref. [8]. On a rectangular cluster that breaks C4C_{4} symmetry, χs\chi_{s} and χcx​y\chi_{c}^{xy} are biased towards stripes in a single direction, similar to the single-band counterpart. By symmetry arguments, χcx​x\chi_{c}^{xx} and χcy​y\chi_{c}^{yy} would show preferred stripe direction even on a square lattice, because it is the induced charge modulation by a perturbation that breaks C4C_{4} symmetry. On a rectangular lattice stripe tendencies, as indicated by these correlation functions, can strengthen or compete with the bias from the lattice geometry, as observed in the following results.

The connected static spin and charge correlations are related to the spin and charge susceptibilities in momentum space via the Fourier transform.

χs(𝐪,ω=0)=1N∑jexp(−i𝐪⋅(𝐫j−𝐫i))χs,i​j(ω=0),\displaystyle\chi_{s}(\mathbf{q},\omega=0)=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{j}\exp{(-i\mathbf{q}\cdot(\mathbf{r}_{j}-\mathbf{r}_{i}))}\chi_{s,ij}(\omega=0),
χcμ​ν(𝐪,ω=0)=1N∑jexp(−i𝐪⋅(𝐫j−𝐫i))χc,i​j(ω=0),\displaystyle\chi_{c}^{\mu\nu}(\mathbf{q},\omega=0)=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{j}\exp{(-i\mathbf{q}\cdot(\mathbf{r}_{j}-\mathbf{r}_{i}))}\chi_{c,ij}(\omega=0),

where μ,ν∈{d,x,y}\mu,\nu\in\set{d,x,y}, which stand for the orbitals dd, pxp_{x}, and pyp_{y}. ii denotes any sites with orbital ν\nu, and jj denotes the summation over all sites with orbital μ\mu. 𝐫i,𝐫j\mathbf{r}_{i},\mathbf{r}_{j} are vectors pointing to the real space coordinate of orbital i,ji,j. When the system is unstable against a spin stripe or charge density wave order, χs​(𝐪)\chi_{s}(\mathbf{q}) or χcμ​ν​(𝐪)\chi_{c}^{\mu\nu}(\mathbf{q}) diverges at the modulation wavevector 𝐪∗\mathbf{q^{*}}. Nevertheless, at finite temperature, observing a double peak structure in momentum space or a stripe-like pattern in real space does not necessarily imply the presence of the other, especially when the real space correlation function shows a stripe pattern but decays quickly or when the momentum space double peak is not extremely sharp.

III.2 Bond charge nematic susceptibility

Upon the formation of a unidirectional stripe, charge transport along the two dd-pp bond directions (xx or yy) is expected to differ. Consider a small anisotropy in tp​dt_{pd}: tp​d→tp​d+δ​tt_{pd}\to t_{pd}+\delta t in the xx direction and tp​d→tp​d−δ​tt_{pd}\to t_{pd}-\delta t in the yy direction. The induced difference between the contributions from the horizontal and vertical d−pd-p bonds to the kinetic energy, which we will call the B1​gB_{1g} kinetic energy anisotropy, is given by

Kp​dx−Kp​dy=−(tp​d+δt)∑i(ξai+ξci)+(tp​d−δt)∑i(ξib+ξid),\displaystyle\begin{split}&K_{pd}^{x}-K_{pd}^{y}\\ =&-(t_{pd}+\delta t)\sum_{i}(\xi^{a}_{i}+\xi^{c}_{i})+(t_{pd}-\delta t)\sum_{i}(\xi_{i}^{b}+\xi_{i}^{d}),\end{split}

which is related to the bond-charge nematic susceptibility by

∂⟨Kp​dx−Kp​dy⟩∂δ​t|δ​t=0=tp​d​χB1​g​(ω=0)+δ​t​⟨Kp​d⟩/tp​d.\displaystyle\frac{\partial\langle K^{x}_{pd}-K^{y}_{pd}\rangle}{\partial\delta t}\Bigg|_{\delta t=0}=t_{pd}\chi_{B_{1g}}(\omega=0)+\delta t\langle K_{pd}\rangle/t_{pd}.

The static B1​gB_{1g} bond-charge nematic susceptibility χB1​g\chi_{B_{1g}} is given by

χB1​g(ω=0)=∂⟨ρB1​g⟩∂δ​t|δ​t=0=∫0β(⟨ρB1​g​(τ)​ρB1​g​(0)⟩−⟨ρB1​g​(τ)⟩​⟨ρB1​g​(0)⟩)​dτ,\displaystyle\begin{split}&\chi_{B_{1g}}(\omega=0)=\frac{\partial\langle\rho_{B_{1g}}\rangle}{\partial\delta t}\Bigg\rvert_{\delta t=0}\\ =&\int_{0}^{\beta}(\langle\rho_{B_{1g}}(\tau)\rho_{B_{1g}}(0)\rangle-\langle\rho_{B_{1g}}(\tau)\rangle\langle\rho_{B_{1g}}(0)\rangle)d\tau,\end{split}

where the ρB1​g\rho_{B_{1g}} operator is defined by

ρB1​g=∑iξia−ξib+ξic−ξid.\displaystyle\begin{split}{\rho}_{B_{1g}}=&\sum_{i}\xi^{a}_{i}-\xi^{b}_{i}+\xi^{c}_{i}-\xi^{d}_{i}.\end{split}

If a stripe forms along the dd-pp direction, a small perturbation in tp​dt_{pd} would induce a finite kinetic energy anisotropy, and χB1​g​(ω=0)\chi_{B_{1g}}(\omega=0) will diverge. Similarly, for a small anisotropy in tp​pt_{pp}, we can deduce a bond-charge nematic susceptibility with B2​gB_{2g} symmetry, χB2​g\chi_{B_{2g}}, where the B2​gB_{2g} bond-charge operator given by

ρB2​g=ξie−ξif+ξig−ξih.\displaystyle\begin{split}\rho_{B_{2g}}&=\xi^{e}_{i}-\xi^{f}_{i}+\xi^{g}_{i}-\xi^{h}_{i}.\\ \end{split}

If a diagonal stripe forms, χB2​g​(ω=0)\chi_{B_{2g}}(\omega=0) should diverge. These susceptibilities provide another way to characterize the tendency to spontaneoutly form a unidirectional stripe in a given direction.

III.3 Numerical simulation

The spin correlation function ⟨Siz​Sjz⟩\langle S_{i}^{z}S_{j}^{z}\rangle and the charge density profile ⟨niμ⟩\langle n_{i}^{\mu}\rangle are measured from density matrix renormalization group (DMRG) ground state calculations on 24×424\times 4 (hole-doping δ∼1/6\delta\sim 1/6 and 1/121/12) or 32×432\times 4 (hole doping δ∼1/8\delta\sim 1/8) clusters in the cylinder geometry with dd and pyp_{y} orbitals terminating the cylinders at both ends, with no dangling pxp_{x} orbitals, for the Ud​d=6U_{dd}=6 eV Emery model. Static spin and charge susceptibilities χs,i​j​(ω=0),χc,i​jμ​ν​(ω=0)\chi_{s,ij}(\omega=0),\chi_{c,ij}^{\mu\nu}(\omega=0) at finite temperatures are measured from determinant quantum Monte Carlo (DQMC) [2, 26, 28] simulations on 16×416\times 4 and 8×88\times 8 clusters with periodic boundary conditions for the three model parameter sets, in order to track stripe periodicity. To examine the tendency to form unidirectional stripes, bond-charge nematic susceptibilities χB1​g​(ω=0)\chi_{B_{1g}}(\omega=0) and χB2​g​(ω=0)\chi_{B_{2g}}(\omega=0) are measured on 8×88\times 8 clusters.

IV Results and Discussion

IV.1 DMRG ground state benchmark

A previous DQMC study on the charge density wave in the Emery model [17] observed weak charge correlations on the oxygen orbitals and a stronger charge density wave tendency on dd orbitals, which is different from the existing ground-state Emery model calculations [29, 8, 25]. To investigate whether the different Emery model parameters contribute to the distinction, we performed a ground-state DMRG simulation for model parameters as in Ref. [17].

Figure 1 shows the staggered spin correlation on copper (left) and spatial fluctuations of the charge density profile (right) from a DMRG calculation of the inner 16 rungs of a 24×424\times 4 (32×432\times 4 for 1/81/8 doping) cylinder at Ud​d=6U_{dd}=6 eV, Up​p=0U_{pp}=0, Δp​d=3\Delta_{pd}=3 eV. The DMRG staggered spin correlations show a shorter spin stripe period with increasing hole doping. Charge accumulates near the AFM domain wall, while being depleted near the center of the cylinder. In panels (b, d, f), the charge densities on d,px,pyd,p_{x},p_{y} orbitals vary concomitantly with a common periodicity, locking to half of the spin stripe period. This charge modulation is strongest on the pyp_{y} orbital and weakest on the dd orbitals. Although this parameter set features smaller Ud​dU_{dd}, Up​pU_{pp}, and Δp​d\Delta_{pd} compared to Refs. [29, 8, 25], the ground states remain qualitatively similar. Nevertheless, the charge modulation amplitude in our calculation is significantly weaker, as detailed by comparisons in Fig. S4.

Although at high temperatures [17] the modulation wavevector 𝐪∗\mathbf{q}^{*} of χcd​d​(𝐪,ω=0)\chi_{c}^{dd}(\mathbf{q},\omega=0) does not follow the Yamada relation, it gives way to a charge density wave with a period locked to twice the spin stripe period in the ground state, which is also present on oxygen components of χc​(𝐪,ω=0)\chi_{c}(\mathbf{q},\omega=0) at finite temperature. This benchmark calculation demonstrates that there is likely no qualitative difference among the three parameter sets we studied, at least with respect to the static charge modulation on oxygen orbitals.

IV.2 Fluctuating charge stripe on pp-orbitals

From DQMC calculations on 16×416\times 4 clusters, the spin stripe pattern is visible in χs,i​j​(ω=0)\chi_{s,ij}(\omega=0) across all three parameter sets, as illustrated by the representative example in Fig. 2 (a). The correlation lengths decrease as JJ decreases and as temperature increases (comprehensive data for all parameter sets are provided in the Supplemental Materials). Similarly, the cross-component χcx​y\chi_{c}^{xy}, which is sensitive to the symmetry breaking of the cluster geometry (see Appendix for detail), exhibits clear stripe patterns across the parameters, with a representative case shown in Fig. 2 (c). Two columns of negative correlation functions are spaced by approximately the size of the antiferromagnetic domain shown in the spin correlation functions, indicating that the doped charges tend to either arrange in lines, or clusters. From the DMRG simulations, the charge rich or deficit regions are balanced in the ground state. Without a loss of generality, we refer to the negatively correlated region as charge accumulation.

For Ud​d=8.5U_{dd}=8.5 eV and Up​p=4.1U_{pp}=4.1 eV, χcy​y\chi_{c}^{yy} and χcx​x\chi_{c}^{xx} display real-space charge stripe patterns along the vertical and horizontal directions, respectively (Fig. 2 (b, d)). This behavior indicates that a perturbation on the local potential of the pxp_{x} orbital tends to induce a charge density wave along the xx direction, even when the cluster geometry favors a charge density wave along the yy direction. Furthermore, the pattern in χcx​x\chi_{c}^{xx} indicates that it is more strongly affected by the symmetry breaking of the local perturbation than by the cluster geometry. This xx-direction pattern is less clear for Ud​d=8.5U_{dd}=8.5 eV and Up​p=0U_{pp}=0 eV, and disappears for Ud​d=6U_{dd}=6 eV at the lowest accessible temperatures. From the DMRG benchmark, we know that the ground-state oxygen charge modulations are qualitatively similar across all three parameter sets. Therefore, the differing responses to local perturbations observed in DQMC at the lowest accessible temperatures likely result from a tradeoff between the intrinsic charge modulation strength and the fermion sign problem.

In momentum space, the modulation vector δS​D​W=|𝐪∗−(π,π)|\delta_{SDW}=|\mathbf{q}^{*}-(\pi,\pi)| extracted from χs​(𝐪,ω=0)\chi_{s}(\mathbf{q},\omega=0) along the Y−MY-M direction by fitting to a periodic double Lorentzian peaked at 𝐪∗\mathbf{q}^{*}, increases with hole doping pp. An example with Up​p=0U_{pp}=0 eV is shown in Fig. 3 (a). For the charge susceptibility, the dd-orbital component χcd​d​(ω=0)\chi_{c}^{dd}(\omega=0) shows two peaks whose separation decreases as pp increases, consistent with previous work [17]. The pp orbital components χcx​y​(ω=0)\chi_{c}^{xy}(\omega=0), χcy​y​(ω=0)\chi_{c}^{yy}(\omega=0), and χcx​x​(ω=0)\chi_{c}^{xx}(\omega=0), exhibit two peaks whose separation increases with increasing pp, or one single peak that broadens or remains unchanged if the two peaks are unresolvable. Generally, the peak separation is largest in χcy​y\chi_{c}^{yy} and smallest in χcx​y\chi_{c}^{xy}. χcx​x\chi_{c}^{xx} shows no double peak structure along the Y−MY-M direction because a perturbation on the pxp_{x} orbital favors a charge stripe along the horizontal direction. Table 1 summarizes the qualitative differences in the static charge correlation functions, viewed from both momentum and real space, with supporting data provided in Fig. S19, S20, and S21 from the Supplementary Materials. Overall, the charge modulation wavevector derived from the oxygen charge correlation functions is proportional to the spin stripe modulation wavevector.

Based on the preceding discussion, χcx​x\chi_{c}^{xx} is likely subject to a competing charge-ordering tendency distinct from that induced by the cluster geometry. Hence, it should be excluded when extracting the charge modulation wavevector for the vertical charge stripes present in 16×416\times 4 clusters. Furthermore, because the ground-state charge modulation on the dd orbitals is significantly weaker than that on the pp orbitals, it is reasonable to focus on the oxygen charge modulation induced by a local perturbation of the pyp_{y} charge transfer potential. This is represented by χcy​y​(𝐪,ω=0)+χcx​y​(𝐪,ω=0)\chi_{c}^{yy}(\mathbf{q},\omega=0)+\chi_{c}^{xy}(\mathbf{q},\omega=0) in Fig. 3 (b), which fits well to the periodic double Lorentzian function, similar to the charge correlation function of the single-band Hubbard model [6]. Figure 3 (c) shows that the modulation wavevector of the spin density wave is approximately half of that of the charge density wave, consistent with an intertwined spin and charge stripe scenario. The relation between the spin density wave wavevector and the hole doping shows that the stripe is partially filled at this temperature. For the other two parameter sets, the charge correlation function does not fit to periodic double Lorentzian peaks as cleanly, and the relation between δCDW/2\delta_{\mathrm{CDW}}/2 and δSDW\delta_{\mathrm{SDW}} is less precise (Fig. S17, S18), likely due to the high temperature or weaker modulation intensity, though they remain approximately proportional.

In short, our DQMC and DMRG results on rectangular clusters demonstrate that the intertwined spin stripes on copper and charge stripes on oxygen are reachable by finite temperature DQMC, at least for Emery models with parameters that favor stronger charge modulation. Furthermore, the direction of the charge stripe, as shown in linear response, could be more sensitive to perturbation on the local potential of oxygen orbitals than the lattice geometry. However, because rectangular lattices break C4C_{4} symmetry, these simulations do not probe the spontaneous tendency to form unidirectional stripes along the d−pd-p bond directions.

IV.3 Temperature evolution of stripes and bond-charge nematicity

Square lattices are essential for measuring the tendency towards unidirectional stripe formation in the d−pd-p bond direction via evolution of the stripe patterns in static correlation functions and B1​gB_{1g} and B2​gB_{2g} bond-charge nematic susceptibilities with decreasing temperature. In this geometry, the pxp_{x}-pyp_{y} component of a static susceptibility is fully C4C_{4} symmetric, whereas the pxp_{x}-pxp_{x} and pyp_{y}-pyp_{y} are related by 90∘90^{\circ} rotation and each breaks C4C_{4} symmetry.

Ideally, the C4C_{4}-symmetric spin and charge density correlation functions showcase the following patterns when there is a tendency to form a unidirectional stripe, which breaks the C4C_{4} symmetry in either the B1​gB_{1g} or B2​gB_{2g} mode. In the B1​gB_{1g} mode, there is a tendency to form a stripe along the dd-pp bond directions. The momentum-space superpositon of modulation wavevectors at (π±δ,π)(\pi\pm\delta,\pi) and (π,π±δ)(\pi,\pi\pm\delta) yields a diamond-like pattern in the staggered spin correlation on dd orbitals, and in χcx​y\chi_{c}^{xy} charge accumulation near the antiferromagnetic domain walls in the χs,i​j∗\chi_{s,ij}^{*}, which is near the corners of our square clusters. In the B2​gB_{2g} mode, there is a tendency to form a stripe along the px−pyp_{x}-p_{y} bond directions. The momentum-space superposition of modulation wavevectors at (π±δ,π±δ)(\pi\pm\delta,\pi\pm\delta) gives square-like antiferromagnetic domains, and the charge density should accumulate near the edges of the square clusters. These criteria identify the tendency to break C4C_{4} symmetry in either a B1​gB_{1g} or B2​gB_{2g} pattern from the otherwise C4C_{4} symmetric spin and charge density correlations.

Figure 4 displays the staggered spin (top row) and pxp_{x}-pyp_{y} charge (bottom row) correlation functions with temperature decreasing from left to right. As seen in panels (a, b, c), lowering the temperature causes the local antiferromagnetic domain in the spin correlations to evolve from a square-like to a diamond-like shape. This evolution indicates a crossover from a tendency to break B2​gB_{2g} to one which brakes B1​gB_{1g} symmetry upon cooling. Concurrently, the charge correlations in panels (d, e, f) show that charge accumulation tendency weakens at the edge-aligned regions around (0,±3)(0,\pm 3) and (±2,0)(\pm 2,0), while strengthening near the corner (±3,±3)(\pm 3,\pm 3). This intensity shift further corroborates the enhanced tendency to form unidirectional charge stripes along the dd-pp bond directions. Overall, Fig. 4 demonstrates that the χc,i​jx​y​(ω=0)\chi_{c,ij}^{xy}(\omega=0) and χs,i​j​(ω=0)\chi_{s,ij}(\omega=0) evolve concomitantly with doping and temperature, at least up to T≃0.2T\simeq 0.2 eV, above which the correlation functions are obscured by statistical noise. This tendency to form spin and charge stripes along the xx or yy directions is observed across other hole-doping levels and three-band parameter sets (see Fig. S22 and S23).

This crossover is further corroborated by the temperature evolution of the B1​gB_{1g} and B2​gB_{2g} bond-charge nematic susceptibilities. Figure 5 (a) and (b) display the static nematic susceptibilities χB1​g​(ω=0)\chi_{B_{1g}}(\omega=0) and χB2​g​(ω=0)\chi_{B_{2g}}(\omega=0) defined in Sec. III. These quantities measure the linear response of the kinetic energy to a small anisotropy in the hopping parameters, but excluding the contribution from the change in hopping parameters to the first order. Panel (a) demonstrates that χB1​g​(ω=0)\chi_{B_{1g}}(\omega=0) grows as temperature decreases, accelerating notably below T≃0.2T\simeq 0.2 eV, which roughly coincides with the emergence of intertwined stripe patterns in the correlation functions. Panel (b) reveals that χB2​g​(ω=0)\chi_{B_{2g}}(\omega=0) generally decreases with decreasing temperature, exhibiting a precipitous drop near T≃0.4T\simeq 0.4 eV. This initial drop corresponds to a rapid, temperature-driven increase in charge transport diffusivity [34]. Below T≃0.1T\simeq 0.1 eV, χB2​g\chi_{B_{2g}} undergoes another sharp downturn, corresponding to the onset of the diamond-like spin and charge stripe patterns observed in Fig. 4. Together, these behaviors suggest that a diverging nematic susceptibility in a single dominant symmetry channel is closely tied to the formation of unidirectional stripes.

Figures 4 and 5 jointly reveal that the dd-orbital spin correlation and oxygen charge correlation are already mutually coupled at around T≃0.2T\simeq 0.2 eV, whereas the spontaneous tendency to form unidirectional stripes along the dd-pp bonds only emerges at lower temperatures (T∼0.1T\sim 0.1 eV) for the Ud​d=6U_{dd}=6 eV parameter set. For the other two parameter sets, the fermion sign problem precludes accessing this low-temperature regime, leaving the B2​gB_{2g} mode still significant at the lowest accessible temperatures. Nevertheless, the temperature evolution of both the nematic susceptibility and spatial correlation functions remains qualitatively similar across all sets within their respective accessible temperature ranges. Comparing across the Emery model parameters, while the Ud​d=8.5U_{dd}=8.5 eV parameter sets does not yet exhibit a spontaneous B1​gB_{1g} stripe tendency on the square lattice at accessible temperatures, it produces more intense charge modulations on the 16×416\times 4 clusters where the C4C_{4} symmetry is externally broken. Consequently, the intrinsic amplitude of the charge modulation and its tendency towards B1​gB_{1g} symmetry breaking must be understood as distinct properties of the intertwined spin and charge stripe.

Having established that the bond-charge nematic susceptibilities – the tendency toward spontaneous kinetic energy anisotropy – is linked to the formation of charge stripes, we now focus on the kinetic energy anisotropy in 16×416\times 4 clusters, where a unidirectional stripe pattern is visible from the static correlation function. As shown in Fig. 6, the normalized kinetic energy anisotropies are negative for hole dopings p>0p>0. This indicates that the kinetic energy is enhanced along the yy-direction, the direction of the antiferromagnetic domain wall, with the anisotropy growing in magnitude as temperature decreases. This finite-temperature observation aligns with ground-state DMRG results [29], which demonstrates that vertical hopping amplitudes are larger than the horizontal ones near the antiferromagnetic domain walls. Notably, the doping dependence of this anisotropy is non-monotonic. For Ud​d=6U_{dd}=6 eV at β=12\beta=12 eV-1, the kinetic energy anisotropy shows a pronounced minimum near p=0.15p=0.15. A similar low-temperature curvature also begins to develop for the Ud​d=8.5U_{dd}=8.5 eV, Up​p=0U_{pp}=0 parameter set. While a comparable non-monotonic doping dependence for nematic susceptibility or stripe tendencies has been observed in the single-band Hubbard model and cuprates [15, 6], a direct connection remains yet to be established between nematic susceptibility and charge stripes. In contrast, our Emery model results demonstrate that the bond-charge nematicity and kinetic energy anisotropy are coupled with the formation of charge stripes.

The pp-orbital preference of the charge modulation and the kinetic energy asymmetry may help elucidate the microscopic origin of the charge stripes. From the perspective of perturbation theory, in the limit of Ud​d→∞U_{dd}\to\infty, one extra hole on a pp orbital in a half-filled Emery model induces a ferromagnetic correlation between its two neighboring dd orbitals. This interaction is due to the effective dd-pp antiferromagnetic exchange given by tp​d2/(Up​p+Δp​d)t_{pd}^{2}/(U_{pp}+\Delta_{pd}) [14], which locally disrupts the antiferromagnetic background. Depending on whether the doped holes primarily occupy the pxp_{x} or pyp_{y} orbitals, two heuristic scenarios can be constructed. Consider a 16×416\times 4 cluster where the antiferromagnetic domain wall is oriented along the yy-direction. If the doped holes were to reside on the pxp_{x} orbitals, the local dd-dd and dd-pp exchange interactions could be largely satisfied, and hole motion along the xx-direction would fluctuate the antiferromagnetic domain wall. However, our numerical results for the Emery model turn out to be different: pyp_{y} orbitals exhibit a higher hole occupation near the antiferromagnetic domain wall than pxp_{x} orbitals, and the kinetic energy along the yy direction is more negative than along the xx direction, which frustrates the antiferromagnetic correlation along the yy-axis. This preference of pyp_{y} occupation indicates that the system gains more kinetic energy through the delocalization along the yy-direction than the transverse fluctuations of the AFM domain walls.

V Conclusions

In summary, we report the real-space observation of intertwined spin and charge stripes at finite temperatures using DQMC on rectangular clusters, finding that they approximately satisfy the Yamada relation. This is achieved through exploring the balance between the fermion sign problem and the intrinsic tendency to form stripes with a few different cuprate-relevant parameter sets. Our ground-state DMRG simulation on 44-leg ladders robustly corroborates these findings; both methods consistently show that the copper dd-orbital spin stripes intertwine with the oxygen charge stripes, and that the charge modulation resides primarily on the pp orbitals oriented parallel to the rivers of charge.

We found that at finite temperatures, particularly for Ud​d=8.5U_{dd}=8.5 eV, a local perturbation to the charge transfer energy induces a charge modulation wavevector perpendicular to the corresponding dd-pp bond, indicating that the charge modulation could be short-ranged and sensitive to impurities. Notably, it could provide a compelling microscopic mechanism for the short-ranged, randomly oriented stripe patches that have been recently observed in STM experiments [32]. Therefore, an interesting problem for future research would be to model the C4C_{4} symmetry-breaking impurities and determine their effect on the charge and spin stripes.

By tracking the temperature evolution of the C4C_{4} symmetric cluster, we uncovered evidence that spin-charge-locking in correlation functions emerges at temperatures significantly higher than the dominance of the B1​gB_{1g} symmetry-breaking tendency. As the system cools, the tendency to develop kinetic energy anisotropy evolves concomitantly with the spin and charge correlation functions. Crucially, when the C4C_{4} symmetry is externally broken, the kinetic energy is enhanced along the antiferromagnetic domain walls. Because the kinetic energy dictates the sum rule for the optical conductivity, this enhancement supports the notion of “rivers of conducting charge” from experimental observations, where intertwined stripes play a key role in charge transport.

Ultimately, establishing this detailed, orbital-resolved picture of fluctuating stripes at finite temperatures bridges a critical gap between ground-state numerical techniques and experimental observations. By demonstrating that the three-band Emery model intrinsically captures these complex, intertwined nematic and stripe phases—and by explicitly connecting the orbital-selective charge modulations to directional transport—our results provide a vital microscopic foundation. Unraveling these intermediate-temperature, symmetry-breaking tendencies is a necessary step toward comprehensively understanding the anomalous normal-state transport, the strange metal regime, and the eventual emergence of superconductivity in strongly correlated hole-doped cuprates.

Appendix A Methods

A.1 Density matrix renormalization group

We have implemented a version of DMRG [30, 18] that respects the S​U​(2)≡S​U​(2)s​p​i​n⊗U​(1)c​h​a​r​g​eSU(2)\equiv SU(2)_{spin}\otimes U(1)_{charge} symmetry of the model, i.e., full spin rotational symmetry and charge conservation. We keep bond dimensions of S​U​(2)SU(2) multiplets up to DD=16,000 (equivalent to m≈47,000m\approx 47,000 U⁡(1)U(1) states). This ensures accurate results with a typical truncation error ϵ≈3×10−7\epsilon\approx 3\times 10^{-7}. The calculations are on a 24×424\times 4 cylinder for 1/61/6 and 1/121/12 hole doping, and 32×432\times 4 cylinder for 1/81/8 hole doping. The doping labeled in the main text is the hole doping counted within the 1616 rungs from the center, which is close to the total hole doping. The charge and spin correlation functions presented are extrapolated to infinite bond dimension.

A.2 Bond charge nematic susceptibilities

In the gauge where the Emery model is manifestly C4C_{4} symmetric, in momentum space, the bond charge nematic susceptibilities explicitly show the form factors for B1​gB_{1g} and B2​gB_{2g} symmetry. Using the gauge transformation as explained in Ref. [34], the bond charge nematic susceptibilities are given by

ρB1​g=∑iξai−ξbi+ξci−ξdi=∑𝐤,σ[2cos(kx/2)(p~𝐤,σx†d~𝐤,σ+d~𝐤,σ†p~𝐤,σx)−2cos(ky/2)(p~𝐤,σy†d~𝐤,σ+d~𝐤,σ†p~𝐤,σy)]\displaystyle\begin{split}{\rho}_{B_{1g}}=&\sum_{i}\xi^{a}_{i}-\xi^{b}_{i}+\xi^{c}_{i}-\xi^{d}_{i}=\sum_{\mathbf{k},\sigma}[2\cos(k_{x}/2)(\widetilde{p}_{\mathbf{k},\sigma}^{x\dagger}\widetilde{d}_{\mathbf{k},\sigma}+\widetilde{d}_{\mathbf{k},\sigma}^{\dagger}\widetilde{p}_{\mathbf{k},\sigma}^{x})-2\cos(k_{y}/2)(\widetilde{p}_{\mathbf{k},\sigma}^{y\dagger}\widetilde{d}_{\mathbf{k},\sigma}+\widetilde{d}_{\mathbf{k},\sigma}^{\dagger}\widetilde{p}_{\mathbf{k},\sigma}^{y})]\end{split}
ρB2​g=ξei−ξfi+ξgi−ξhi=∑𝐤4sin(kx/2)sin(ky/2)(p~𝐤,σx†p~𝐤,σy+p~𝐤,σy†p~𝐤,σx)\displaystyle\begin{split}\rho_{B_{2g}}&=\xi^{e}_{i}-\xi^{f}_{i}+\xi^{g}_{i}-\xi^{h}_{i}=\sum_{\mathbf{k}}4\sin(k_{x}/2)\sin(k_{y}/2)(\tilde{p}_{\mathbf{k},\sigma}^{x\dagger}\tilde{p}_{\mathbf{k},\sigma}^{y}+\tilde{p}_{\mathbf{k},\sigma}^{y\dagger}\tilde{p}_{\mathbf{k},\sigma}^{x})\end{split}

A.3 Determinant quantum Monte Carlo

DQMC is numerically exact but limited by the fermion sign problem. The fermion sign of the Emery model depends on the parameters, and gets smaller when Ud​dU_{dd}, Up​pU_{pp}, Δp​d\Delta_{pd} increase or the temperature decreases. Figure S1 shows the average sign.

Due to the exponentially decaying charge correlation signal and the slow convergence, we do not explore a regime with even smaller average sign. The number of measurement sweeps and Markov chains is shown in Table 2. Doping levels are tuned by adjusting the chemical potential to the accuracy of ∼10−4\sim 10^{-4} in the average density.

Jackknife resampling is used to estimate the standard errors. The spacing in the imaginary time grid δ​τ≤0.05\delta\tau\leq 0.05~eV-1 for all simulations with Ud​d=8.5U_{dd}=8.5 eV and δ​τ≤0.08\delta\tau\leq 0.08~eV -1 for some simulations with Ud​d=6U_{dd}=6 eV.

A.4 Monte Carlo sampling

In a system with translational symmetry, χi​j=χi′​j′\chi_{ij}=\chi_{i^{\prime}j^{\prime}} if 𝐫𝐢−𝐫j=𝐫i′−𝐫j′\mathbf{r_{i}}-\mathbf{r}_{j}=\mathbf{r}_{i^{\prime}}-\mathbf{r}_{j^{\prime}}, where i,i′i,i^{\prime} and j,j′j,j^{\prime} belong to the same type of orbital. For the charge correlation function, although ⟨ni​(τ)⟩=⟨ni​(0)⟩\langle n_{i}(\tau)\rangle=\langle n_{i}(0)\rangle, the Monte Carlo samples for different time slices are generally different. The correlation function for each time slice are evaluated by ⟨ni​(τ)​nj​(0)⟩−⟨ni​(τ)⟩​⟨nj​(0)⟩\langle n_{i}(\tau)n_{j}(0)\rangle-\langle n_{i}(\tau)\rangle\langle n_{j}(0)\rangle from the Monte Carlo data, which reduces the number of samples required compared to other estimators of the orbital resolved density. In addition, we utilized all spatial symmetries and the symmetry given by the cyclic property of the trace ⟨ni​(τ)​nj​(0)⟩=⟨nj​(β−τ)​ni​(0)⟩\langle n_{i}(\tau)n_{j}(0)\rangle=\langle n_{j}(\beta-\tau)n_{i}(0)\rangle, which further reduces the statistical error.

A.5 Symmetry of correlation functions

Due to the C2C_{2} point group symmetry of the oxygen orbitals in the Emery model, the pxp_{x}-pxp_{x} and pyp_{y}-pyp_{y} components of the charge correlation functions have C2C_{2} symmetry, where the C4C_{4} symmetry is explicitly broken by the perturbation of the charge transfer energy on pxp_{x} or pyp_{y} orbitals, but they are related by 90 degree rotation to each other. On a C4C_{4} symmetric square lattice, we can rotate our coordinate system and exchange the pxp_{x} and pyp_{y} orbital labels, i.e. χc,i​jx​y​(ω=0)=χc,π⁡(i)​π​(j)y​x​(ω=0)\chi_{c,ij}^{xy}(\omega=0)=\chi_{c,\pi(i)\pi(j)}^{yx}(\omega=0), where π⁡(⋅)\pi(\cdot) maps the orbital location in the original coordinate system to a new coordinate system with a 90∘90^{\circ} rotation. The cyclic property of trace implies that we have χc,i​jx​y​(ω=0)=χc,j​iy​x​(ω=0)\chi_{c,ij}^{xy}(\omega=0)=\chi_{c,ji}^{yx}(\omega=0). Comparing the two equalities above, we know that χc,i​jx​y\chi_{c,ij}^{xy} is symmetric under 90∘90^{\circ} rotation, and hence C4C_{4} symmetric.

A.6 Finite size effect

We simulate a few dopings near the lowest accessible temperatures, limited by the Fermion sign problem for 10×1010\times 10 clusters with Ud​d=6U_{dd}=6 eV and Ud​d=8.5U_{dd}=8.5 eV (Up​p=0U_{pp}=0). The staggered static spin correlation functions and oxygen charge correlation functions are shown in Fig. S2 and S3. The χcy​y\chi_{c}^{yy} is qualitatively similar to the 8×88\times 8 clusters at the lowest accessible temperatures, which show positive charge correlation regions above and below the reference point, but even clearer. χcx​y\chi_{c}^{xy} for Ud​d=6U_{dd}=6 eV shows the B1​gB_{1g} and B2​gB_{2g} patterns, while the signal for Ud​d=8.5U_{dd}=8.5 eV, Up​p=0U_{pp}=0 is mostly below the large error bar, but is not in contradiction to the 8×88\times 8 data.
